before: pre marks preformatted text: spaces and line breaks matter. code marks computer code. They have different jobs, so pre can wrap code when both apply. Ordinary paragraphs normally collapse runs of spaces for display.

pre does not turn HTML parsing off. Use already-learned character references for angle brackets that should be text. Keep a wanted first character immediately after the opening tag: HTML treats a newline immediately after a pre start tag specially by ignoring that first newline.

This example contains a real line break and two spaces before second. ```html 
first
  second
``` The text content is first, a newline, two spaces, then second. pre preserves that layout purpose; code supplies code semantics. Neither element executes the text.

Write open, then a newline and two spaces before save, then a newline and close. Do not use repeated br elements to simulate the stored code text. The task tests exact text content, not font or screen dimensions.
after: `<pre>` keeps the spaces and line breaks you type. That helps when the layout of the text matters. Put `<code>` inside it to mark the text as a code sample. These tags show the sample; they do not run it.

HTML tags still work inside `<pre>`. To show angle brackets as text, use `<` for `<` and `>` for `>`. Keep the first wanted character right after the opening tags so you do not add an extra blank line.

This sample keeps two lines and two spaces before the second word. ```html 
first
  second
``` `
` keeps the layout. `` marks the sample as code. The line break moves `second` onto a new line. The two spaces move it a little to the right.
